author: Page
name_in_asr: Nalanda; monasteries seen by Yuan Chwang
asr_identification: Nalanda (Bargaon): which pre-Devapala structure Xuanzang saw not yet determinable; monasteries had at least two storeys
evidence: Monastery 1: Devapala copper-plate (9th c.) in the 3rd of its structures, so Xuanzang's monastery lies below; Monastery 4: stone column-base lying on the collapsed roof concrete of the E verandah proves an upper storey; walls 8-12 ft thick and wide dog-legged stairs
quote: Which of the earlier structures below the Devapala stratum was seen by Yuan Chwang on his pilgrimage here in the early 7th century, it is as yet not possible to say … Yuan Chwang, according to Beal, describes those he saw as being four storeys high … is conclusive evidence that at least a second storey, if no more, existed in this monastery of Devapala's period.
note: Fits Xuanzang's (via the Life) account of multi-storeyed monasteries; dates his Nalanda to below the 9th-c. stratum. Agrees with Mizutani (Bargaon) and the survey (Cunningham); no change in location.

author: Chandra
name_in_asr: Nalanda; Kusagarapura, old Rajagriha; New Rajagriha
asr_identification: Nalanda (Bargaon); old Rajagriha (Kusagarapura) = the hill-girt city of Rajgir, New Rajagriha close to it on the N
evidence: Nalanda 1935-36: sealing with Deer and Wheel and Pala legend Sri Na[landa?] Dharmapaladeva; Gupta sealing with Deer and Wheel; coin moulds of Narasimhagupta Baladitya. Rajgir: Maniyar Math in the centre of the old city excavated 12 ft below the 1908 circular structure, two earlier strata with enclosures of 17x12x2 in. bricks (pre-Christian era)
quote: with the Deer and the Wheel of Law symbol, below which is a … three-line inscription in Pāla script, giving the legend Sri Na (or Nālandā?) Dharmapāladera … Kuśāgārapura and old Rājagriba. Ajātasatru, the son and successor of king Bimbisāra of the Saisunaga dynasty of Magadha, is said to have founded New Rājagriha close to the site of old Rājagriha and to its north.
note: Agrees with Mizutani (Bargaon; old Rajagrha in the hill-ringed valley, new city outside its N gate) and with the survey (Cunningham, ASR I). The sealing reading is tentative; the Rajgir identifications are taken as given, with new stratigraphy at Maniyar Math.

author: Chandra
asr_identification: Gonsai Khanda brickfield, Sandalpur village, N of the road to Kumrahar and Bulandibagh near Patna: part of ancient Pataliputra

quote: trial excavations were carried out in a brickfield locally known as Gonsai Khanda, situated in the village Sandalpur near the Arzani Dargah to the north of the road to Kumrahar and Bulandibagh near Patna … The Bulandibagh pieces might well have formed part of the old wooden palisade of Pățaliputra
note: Adds a third Mauryan timber site E of Patna (with Kumrahar and Bulandibagh); against the NW-of-Patna placing in Mizutani's gloss, and E of the survey's Bhika Pahari (Beglar, ASR VIII).

author: Srivastava
asr_identification: Maheswar on the N bank of the Narmada, 28 miles W of Barwaha station (Indore State)
evidence: old deposits c. 30 ft below the top near Mandel Khoh on the N bank: coarse pottery, grooved roof tiles, bricks 20x11x3 in. taken to go back to the 6th c. A.D.
quote: Maheswar which is 28 miles to the west of Barwaha Railway Station is picturesquely situated on the north bank of the Narmadā … The place was visited by Hiuen Tsang (7th Century A.D.) and also by Al Biruni (11th Century A.D.) who calls it Mahmura.
note: Asserted, not argued (by the name). Differs from Mizutani (Gwalior region, majority view, disputed), from the survey (Cunningham, Seronj NE of Bhilsa, ASR IX) and from Cunningham's Mandla for Mahishmati, which Srivastava cites.

author: Sahni
asr_identification: Bairat (Jaipur State): the excavated Buddhist site on the hill SW of the valley (Bijak-ki-pahari) is not Xuanzang's Paryatra with eight monasteries
evidence: Jaipur State excavation 1935-36: circular brick temple, debris of two Asokan pillars of Chunar sandstone, a single monastery rebuilt twice with a hoard of 36 silver coins (8 punch-marked, 28 Greek/Indo-Greek, Heliokles to Hermaios), nothing later than 2nd c. A.D.; final destruction probably by the Huns
quote: M. Renaud identified Bairat with Po-le-ye-to-lo of the Chinese pilgrim Hiuen Tsang. My own excavations yielded no evidence to corroborate this identification. The discovery of only one monastery in place of the eight mentioned by the Chinese pilgrim in connection with Po-le-ye-to-lo seems to militate strongly against M. Renaud's view.
note: Against Mizutani (Bairat, agreed) and against the survey (Cunningham, ASR II: Bairat, Bijak hill ruins = two of the eight monasteries). Sahni allows that the town mound, 2 miles off, may hold Buddhist strata. Abandonment c. 2nd c. A.D. also tells against a living monastic site in the 7th c.
